title: The clumsy footman
hook: before the monastery he was an awkward servant who broke everything, and he expected to be punished for it
tomorrow: can turning an omelette in a pan be a prayer?

segments.voice: Yesterday, a bare tree in winter, and the spring Lawrence saw in it. Your line was spring will come. Today, what he was like before any of that.

Coffee across the laptop. The glass that slides off the counter in slow motion. The text sent to the wrong group chat. Everyone has a clumsy streak; some people have a clumsy life. Before the monastery, Brother Lawrence worked as a footman, a household servant who waited at table and carried things. And by his own account, he was terrible at it. He told his visitor plainly: he was a great awkward fellow who broke everything. So what does a man like that expect when he knocks on a monastery door?
screen: `THE GLASS IN SLOW MOTION.` → `A FOOTMAN.` → `HE BROKE EVERYTHING.`

segments.voice: Notice who's telling it. Nobody is mocking Lawrence here. It's Lawrence himself, describing the servant he used to be, with no shame and no excuse. Then the surprising part. He wanted to enter a monastery, he said, thinking he'd be made to suffer there for his awkwardness and for the faults he'd commit. He planned to give God his life, with all its pleasures, as a kind of payment. And God, he said, disappointed him. In that life he met with nothing but satisfaction. The punishment he braced for never came. And what stayed the same? Nothing in the story says he grew graceful first. The clumsiness came with him through the door. He didn't have to earn the place by improving. That's the quiet gift of this page: a life with God that doesn't begin with getting better at things. Lawrence comes as he is, still dropping things, and finds himself welcome. The Psalms say something like it, in the Douay-Rheims: "For he knoweth our frame. He remembereth that we are dust." Here's one to tell a friend tonight: a classic about living in God's presence comes from a man who, by his own account, broke everything.
screen: `HE TELLS IT HIMSELF.` · `EXPECTING PUNISHMENT.` · `GOD DISAPPOINTED HIM.` · `HE KNOWETH OUR FRAME.` · then, large: `HE BROKE EVERYTHING.`

segments.voice: Rest your hands open on your knees, palms up. Bring to mind one clumsy moment you still wince at, the spill, the stumble, the wrong word, and set it in your open hands. Leave them open while the sit runs: nothing to grip, nothing to fix.
The clumsy footman. Lawrence before the monastery: an awkward servant who broke everything, by his own account, and was welcome anyway.
Here's today's line: he broke everything, and he was welcomed anyway, just as he was. Go gently tonight.

howItsDone: Catholic readers of Brother Lawrence often take comfort that he describes his own clumsiness so plainly; the story is read as an invitation to begin a life with God as one already is.

fork.setup: your little brother's first week at a restaurant job: he dropped two plates and wants to quit before they fire him. what does Lawrence's story say?

quit first: being clumsy means the job was never for him.

fork.reveal: Lawrence braced to be punished for his awkwardness and met welcome instead. he didn't need to be graceful first.

chat.meaning: Lawrence called himself an awkward fellow who broke everything. He expected punishment and found welcome. Clumsiness isn't a verdict on you.
